strengths: The paper addresses a useful question for researchers studying visual robustness: which unseen orientations permit successful recognition? Its orientation-resolved accuracy maps reveal patterns that aggregate accuracy would obscure.

The fully-seen/restricted-seen paradigm provides useful experimental control. Holding training-set size constant and evaluating the same restricted-seen instances helps interpret the effects of increasing fully-seen instance diversity.

The experimental coverage is substantial: four architectures, five orientation distributions, multiple object categories, and additional checks involving augmentation, training-set size, scale, and symmetry. These experiments support a recurring association between successful generalization and in-plane similarity.

The rendered examples overlaid on accuracy heatmaps communicate the main observation effectively. The small-angle and in-plane components also provide an interpretable framework for describing the results.
weaknesses: Necessary: narrow the central claim that DNNs are 'only capable' of generalizing to orientations resembling in-plane rotations. The experiments establish a tendency in the tested instance-classification settings, rather than an exclusive capability boundary. Correlation with the proposed model does not establish negligible recognition outside its favored regions, particularly when several reported correlations are modest. Either quantify accuracy and uncertainty outside explicitly defined small-angle/in-plane regions or frame the conclusion as a predominant empirical pattern. The qualification in Section 7 should also be reflected in the abstract and introduction.

Necessary: reconcile the model specification with the reported results. Section 4 defines a sigmoid with inputs in [0,1] but searches over offset b >= 1, so its outputs cannot exceed 0.5, contrary to the explanation about matching high accuracies. Figure 4c also shows approximately 0.6 correlation for AE versus 0.85 for A alone for airplanes rotating on alpha at N=10. Under the stated independent parameter search and maximum construction, suppressing E should allow AE to approximate A alone. These discrepancies may reflect documentation or fitting details, but they need resolution before the component comparisons can be assessed confidently.

Necessary: distinguish descriptive fitting from predictive validation. Section 4 selects parameters to maximize the same correlation used to evaluate the model, without describing an independent evaluation set. This is legitimate evidence of descriptive fit, but does not independently validate prediction. Specify the fitting and evaluation protocol, and either evaluate on held-out observations or restrict the predictive claims accordingly.

Necessary: complete the evaluation details. Appendix B reports 200K images per dataset but does not clearly specify test-set sizes, separation of in-distribution training and test images, observations per orientation bin, or handling of empty bins. It also selects learning rates using OoD behavior without identifying a separate validation set. These omissions limit reproducibility and assessment of the reported accuracy maps and correlations.

Optional improvements: additional repetitions would strengthen the cross-category experiment, which currently uses one trial, and a directly accessible code/data release would facilitate verification. Clarifying that uniform Euler-angle sampling is not uniform over SO(3) would also help readers interpret the aggregate accuracies. Broader real-image experiments would be useful extensions, but are not prerequisites for publishing appropriately scoped findings.
